To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) PDTC is an uncommon thyroid cancer that is associated with an intermediate prognosis between well‐differentiated thyroid cancer (WDTC) and anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (ATC), and (2) the diagnosis of PD TC is based on histologic criteria, which are difficult to apply on FNA specimens.

poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma (PDTCT) is a rare thyroid carcinoma that has a natural history and pathological characteristics that are intermediate between those of anaplastic thyroid carcinoma and well‐differentiated thyroid carcinoma, and that the cytologic diagnosis of this entity is challenging.
poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma is a follicular-cell derived tumor with an intermediate natural history and pathological feature between well-differentiated and undifferentied (anaplastic).

the cytological features of PDTC and their potential role in the preoperative diagnosis and management of patients with PDTC.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
PDTC can be suspected but not definitely diagnosed on cytology.
, in the absence of specific criteria, PDTC is unlikely to be diagnosed on FNA cytology, but the diagnosis should not be excluded on cytological grounds alone.
PDTC is a rare tumour that should be suspected on FNA cytology in cases showing high‐grade cytological features, including marked nuclear atypia and mitotic activity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cytological features of PDTC can be recognised in some cases, but the definitive diagnosis of PDCT requires histological evaluation.

the diagnosis of PDCT in cytology specimens should be based on a combination of cytological features and molecular testing, which is currently not possible in many centres, especially those in developing countries.
cytologic diagnosis of poorly differentiated carcinoma is a challenge.
The main takeaway from our work is that
PDTC should be included as a differential diagnosis in the workup of thyroid lesions with atypia or follicular neoplasm on cytology.
PDTC is not a diagnosis that can be rendered on cytology alone, and a definitive diagnosis can only be made on histology, based on histological criteria that have been proposed.

, despite the fact that PDTC has been recognised as a distinct clinicopathological entity by the World health Organisation, its diagnosis on FNA material is challenging and should only be rendered after a careful review of the cytopathology report in the context of a multidisciplinary discussion.
